transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-10
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jane (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Aurelia Platform), Markus (Aurelia CTO), Elena (Aurelia ML)

Summary (auto):
- Deep dive into KV-layer behavior during long-context runs; repeated evictions and apparent thrashing when clients reuse long prefixes across sessions.
- Discussed paging/eviction, prefetch heuristics, batching impacts, and on-prem/VPC memory tuning.
- Agreed on repro steps and short-term config experiments.

Topics (auto):
- KV cache eviction patterns and metrics
- Paging latency vs throughput tradeoffs
- Prefix reuse optimization and prefetch strategies
- Batching and quantization interactions
- VPC/on-prem memory tuning and kernel limits

Transcript:
[00:00] Jane: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda: we wanna get to the root cause of the KV-layer thrash you saw, walk through logs, and propose config changes. can everyone hear me?
[00:14] Priya: Yep, loud and clear. thanks for making time. we've been seeing these stalls in production — throughput drops and a ton of evictions in the KV cache.
[00:28] Liam: Cool, can you give a short recap of the symptom set? i think you mentioned long prefixes being reused across many sessions?
[00:40] Markus: Yeah, so our docs assistant holds a ~25k token context across users, and many sessions share common prefix headers. what we see is after a few minutes load goes crazy — eviction rate spikes, and tail latency increases from ~120ms to multiple seconds.
[00:56] Elena: And it's intermittent; sometimes it's fine for hours, then we get a cascade of evictions. we've captured some metrics — i'll share shortly.
[01:10] Jane: Great. quick note — transcript auto-caption may mangle some tech words, like K/V cache becoming K V cash, so sorry in advance. let's pull up the eviction metrics first.
[01:22] Priya: (screen share) here's staging: kv_cache_size is 16GB, eviction policy is LRU by default, page_size is 4MB, and we have prefix_reuse=true. hit_rate hovers ~62% but when incidents happen hit_rate tanks to ~18% and evictions/sec goes to thousands.
[01:41] Liam: ok, that lines up with classic thrashing. two quick suspects: one, the working set + prefix reuse pattern exceeds effective cache capacity, causing constant churn; two, prefetch/paging heuristics may be pushing pages that collide with live working set.
[01:58] Priya: Is there a way to see per-prefix residency? our logs show generic evictions but not which prefixes are getting evicted most.
[02:09] Liam: We emit per-key residency in advanced tracing — but on hosted we aggregate. for a repro we can enable per-prefix debug traces for staging. it'll add overhead but worth it.
[02:20] Markus: Is there a known issue with page_size being too small causing more metadata overhead? we set 4MB conservatively to avoid fragmentation.
[02:31] Jane: Smaller page_size increases metadata and higher chance of cross-page eviction. with large long-contexts, sometimes 8–16MB pages reduce churn, but that depends on model's KV footprint.
[02:44] Elena: We're also using dynamic batching with max_tokens_per_batch=2048; could batching patterns be amplifying eviction frequency?
[02:54] Liam: Yes, batching can change access patterns: large batches can force colder KV pages into memory simultaneously. we usually recommend a combo of prefix locality-aware batching and adaptive prefetch.
[03:08] Priya: Can you explain adaptive prefetch? we have prefetch_enabled=true but it seems naive.
[03:16] Liam: Our adaptive prefetch looks at recent access heat for prefixes and tries to pull adjacent KV pages ahead of the request. naive prefetch will pull broad ranges causing noise. the heuristics matter: threshold for 'hot' prefixes, max lookahead pages, and backoff when evictions rise.
[03:33] Jane: Quick pointer — we'll share the prefetch tuning doc after this call. it's been helpful for other customers with long shared prefixes.
[03:42] Priya: When the thrash happens what metrics should we capture? we have CPU, GPU, but not detailed memory pressure on the RAM side.
[03:51] Liam: Capture: kv_cache_hit_rate, kv_cache_evictions/sec, KV page loads/sec, page_faults (if paging to disk enabled), system free memory, GPU mem pressure, and per-request KV latency percentiles. also snapshot the kernel dmesg if OOM killer events triggered.
[04:11] Markus: We run in a VPC with EBS-backed ephemeral storage on our private deployment — paging to disk is allowed. could disk latency be part of the tail?
[04:21] Liam: Definitely. Paging to disk adds 5–50ms+ per page depending on EBS type; if many pages miss at once tail can blow up. for on-prem, disk speeds vary a lot.
[04:31] Priya: We saw occasional IO spikes during incidents. ok that tracks. what about eviction_policy tuning? we use LRU but would something like frequency-adaptive work?
[04:42] Liam: LRU is simple but not always ideal for prefix reuse. LFU or a TinyLFU hybrid can help keep frequently reaccessed prefixes resident. another approach is segmented LRU where recent heavy-use prefixes are protected.
[04:56] Elena: Is there support for pinning prefixes? some of our system headers are critical.
[05:03] Liam: Yes, we have an API to 'pin' keys or mark them as protected for eviction for a TTL. it's additive — good for pinned system tokens like long headers.
[05:13] Priya: We didn't know about pinning; that could be low-effort win.
[05:18] Jane: Action: Liam will show how to pin in staging and we'll provide a short snippet.
[05:25] (brief cross talk)
[05:30] Markus: Another thought — quantization: we're using int8 models; could quant noise expand KV size unexpectedly?
[05:39] Liam: Quantization changes model parameters but should not change key-value cache size directly: KV caches store activations not weights. however quantization can cause tokenization shift or longer intermediate sequences in rare cases — unlikely primary cause. worth validating though.
[05:55] Elena: ok. regarding long-context, some prefixes are 18–27k tokens; do you have guidance on trimming or compacting?
[06:06] Liam: Two quick patterns: prefix compaction (hash and store canonicalized summary tokens) or chunking where you only keep the most recent N tokens in KV and rely on a short summary prefix. both have tradeoffs for fidelity.
[06:20] Priya: We prefer fidelity, customers expect exact history. compaction may be risky.
[06:25] Jane: note: we also discussed a lightweight 'sparse-residency' mode in the runtime — it keeps probabilistic references for very long tails and materializes on demand. it's experimental but helped another customer reduce evictions. we'll indicate stability in the doc.
[06:44] Priya: We're keen to try the staged experiments you mentioned. what’s the minimal repro we should run?
[06:51] Liam: Repro recipe: 1) spin up staging with same kv_cache_size (16GB) and page_size 4MB, 2) load a workload with 30k token contexts and repeated reuse of a set of ~50 prefixes across sessions, 3) ramp to target concurrency while capturing kv metrics and per-prefix residency.
[07:10] Elena: We can produce anonymized prefixes. i'll scrub PHI.
[07:15] Priya: timeline? can you run this on our staging?
[07:18] Liam: We can run it from Redwood side if you grant a temporary access role, otherwise we'll give you an exact client-side load script.
[07:27] Markus: Security-wise we prefer client-side; send the script.
[07:31] Jane: noted — Liam will send the script and we’ll include the debug trace toggles.
[07:36] Priya: A couple more questions — what about GC/cleanup intervals? could aggressive cleanup be kicking in on the KV allocator?
[07:46] Liam: Yes, our allocator has two knobs: aggressive_cleanup_interval and cold_eviction_threshold. setting aggressive interval too small can cause frequent background evictions. we generally set cleanup to 60s for long-context workloads.
[07:59] Elena: do you recommend increasing kv_cache_size instead?
[08:03] Liam: If you can, yes. doubling to 32GB or adding a node with more RAM will reduce churn. but we know budget constraints matter so tuning prefetch + pinning + eviction policy often gives big wins without doubling memory.
[08:16] Priya: For on-prem, are there kernel limits we should watch? we've hit semaphores and file descriptor limits before.
[08:23] Liam: ulimit, file-descriptor counts, and hugepage settings matter. for our runtime we recommend hugepages enabled for large KV allocations and setting vm.swappiness low if you want to avoid OS swapping. we'll share a checklist.
[08:36] Jane: we'll add hugepage guidance to the follow-up.
[08:40] (short pause)
[08:45] Markus: Logging noise: when we enable per-prefix traces the logs get huge; any sampling recommendations?
[08:51] Liam: Sample at 0.1–1% for continuous production traces and 100% for short repro windows. also use aggregated histograms rather than per-event logs where possible.
[09:03] Priya: okay. about the prefetch heuristic: you mentioned lookahead pages and backoff. what are conservative default values?
[09:11] Liam: Default safe values: lookahead=1–2 pages, max_prefetch_parallel=2, hot_threshold=10 accesses in last 60s, backoff_factor increase TTL for that prefix if eviction/sec rises > 50% baseline.
[09:27] Elena: that seems reasonable. we'll try more conservative ones first.
[09:31] Jane: quick architecture note — our runtime does kernel selection for kv page handling; some kernels are optimized for contiguous page access vs random. your access pattern determines perf. we can profile kernel usage in the trace.
[09:47] Markus: If kernels expect contiguous access and we have random access, can that blow up CPU or GPU time?
[09:53] Liam: It can blow CPU time for page assemble and increase latency. Profiling will show whether pages are being stitched frequently.
[10:02] Priya: Anything else we should consider re batching and quantization?
[10:07] Liam: For batching: prefer smaller batch sizes with higher batch frequency if latency SLO is tight; for throughput optimize using batching with KV locality-aware grouping. Quantization: monitor for tokenization changes but it's a lower priority.
[10:21] Elena: Are there any quick experiments we should run right now during this call?
[10:25] Liam: We could try toggling page_size to 8MB in staging and run a short workload for 10 minutes to see eviction patterns; but we need to coordinate.
[10:34] Markus: We don't have staging perms live here. do it offline.
[10:37] Jane: we'll schedule the short experiment — I'll add it to next steps.
[10:42] Priya: Are there known regressions in the runtime recently that could explain new thrashing? we upgraded runtime last month.
[10:50] Liam: There was a change to prefetch backoff heuristics in the last release — it was intended to be safer but under certain prefix-reuse patterns it could over-fetch. we thought we covered it but good to validate against your workload.
[11:05] Elena: can you point to the release note?
[11:08] Liam: yes — I'll paste the PR link in the follow-up.
[11:12] Markus: ok. one last question: what SLOs are reasonable after tuning? we're shooting for p95 < 200ms and throughput stable under concurrency 120.
[11:22] Liam: With the right tuning and maybe raising cache to 32GB, p95 < 200ms is achievable; without extra memory, we aim for p95 < 500ms with tuned prefetch and pinning.
[11:33] Priya: thanks. let's recap next steps.
[11:36] Jane: Recap: 1) Liam will hand over client-side load script + repro recipe; 2) Priya/Elena to provide anonymized prefix traces; 3) Run staging experiments: (a) increase page_size to 8MB, (b) toggle pinning on critical prefixes, (c) try segmented LFU eviction.
[11:56] Liam: I'll also enable per-prefix debug traces for a short window once you run the script, and share the metric dashboards.
[12:08] Priya: thanks — we'll aim to get traces to you by 2025-04-12.
[12:12] Jane: i'll send the follow-up with config snippets and the prefetch doc by 2025-04-11.
[12:18] Markus: thanks everyone.
[12:20] (meeting ends)
